The project has 3 main components: i) civil works component which focuses on improving critical state highways through conventional item rate contracts and delivery of one road through a modern contracting method (components A1 & A2); ii) Road safety component which focuses on interventions to improve safety for vulnerable road users (component B), and iii) road sector modernization which seeks to frame and steer engineering, financial and organizational measures to improve the long term management of roads and create a center of excellence within the road sector (component C).

The project ratings for implementation progress and achievement of development objective have both been retained as Moderately Unsatisfactory (MU) as the project is progressing behind schedule and the achievement of PDO could be significantly delayed. While component A1 is fully committed and shows 85% progress, component A2 is not yet committed (although procurement has been initiated), component B is 60% committed (procurement in progress for 10%), and component C is 20% committed (procurement in progress for remaining). The project has 3 main components: i) civil works component which focusses on improving critical state highways through conventional item rate contracts and delivery of one road through a PPP concession; ii) Road safety component which focusses on interventions to improve safety for vulnerable road users, and iii) road sector modernization which seeks to frame and steer engineering, financial and organizational measures to improve the long term management of roads and move the overall approach from 'road building' to 'road asset management and delivery of road services to end users'. The aim of the mid term review mission was to take stock of the overall direction of the project and assess requirements for course correction, if needed. The likelihood of achieving the Project Development Objective (DO) is still good. Despite initial implementation delays, progress of physical works under the first component - which is a significant part of the investments - have improved. Hence the overall implementation progress has been upgraded from Moderately Unsatisfactory to Moderately Satisfactory. There are still a number of operational challenges in this main civil works component, however, the main challenge is a lack of full time project director. It is critical that a full time project director is appointed to deal with day to day operational decisions and to steer all parties towards improvement in implementation progress.

The Government of Kerala made a number of important decisions which have led to improvements in the progress of the road projects. However, to sustain these improvements, a dedicated full time project director is needed. The procurement of the PPP project is on-going. After several delays resulting from the need to obtain clearances from various Government of Kerala departments, this PPP road is now at qualification stage. The Government of Kerala has offered assurances to ensure progress of this aspect of the project and move towards financial close according to an agreed time-frame. A major concern is the progress of the non-civil works components of the project i.e. road safety and road sector modernization. After starting off well, the road safety component has stalled. The main challenge is related to delays in staffing of the Kerala Road Safety Authority. This is having a knock-on effect on dependent activities such as the capacity building and road safety proposals for the challenge fund. The road sector modernization component has finally started taking shape. Procurement of consultancies needed to underpin critical decisions are underway and should be finalized by July 2016. The main challenge in this component is the slow pace of progress on stakeholder engagement, constituting the review group (made up of public and private individuals), and appointment of a technical advisor to support the program.

The Government of Kerala has been advised to revisit the framework for representing client interests and driving the strategic road network program - which is a principal part of this component. CONTEXT AT APPRAISAL Context 1. The state of Kerala has one of the highest human development outcomes in India. It is also a highly urbanized state, with almost half1 of its population living in urban areas. The economy is heavily dependent on the tertiary sector, which accounts for 65 percent of its Gross Value Added. Remittances remain the primary driver for Kerala’s economy, and account for 25 percent of the state’s Gross Domestic Product. 2. The World Bank has been engaged in the road sector in Kerala since the first Kerala State Transport Project (KSTP) was approved in 2002. KSTP had a focus on physical infrastructure (for transport corridor upgrading, road maintenance, and improving road safety) as well as measures to improve institutional capacity and processes for managing the road network. In addition to substantial achievements on infrastructure works for road upgrading, the project accomplished several tasks that were intended to improve the institutional and financial capacity of the state's transport sector institutions. A dedicated independent Road Safety Authority and a Road Safety Fund were set up in the state. KSTP’s institutional strengthening component also laid the foundation for a sustainable road asset management system and helped develop a Road Development Policy.

Encouraged by the successful implementation of KSTP, Government of Kerala (GOK) initiated the preparation of the next phase, based on which the Bank engaged with GOK on the preparation of the Second Kerala State Transport Project (KSTP-II). 3. At the time of appraisal of KSTP-II (2012-13), Kerala had a total road network of 152,000 km, of which about 70 percent of the State Highways (SH) were single lane; of these, 54 percent were in poor condition. Despite a dense2 and extensive road network relative to its geographical size, the poor quality and sub-optimal alignment of many roads were constraining the state’s development. The dense population and ribbon development along the main transport links had resulted in dispersed settlement patterns leading to traffic congestion in this state. The state resembles a rural-urban continuum, which the State Planning Commission has termed ‘rurban’ development. One of the other challenges facing the Kerala roads sector at appraisal was an incomplete state-level framework for funding and financing road sector investments particularly given the estimated financing gap upwards of US$700 million per year between investment needs and anticipated revenues. GOK was contemplating the best way to involve the private sector in this framework. This was the genesis for the introduction of a subcomponent on annuity-style PPP for financing, asset development, and maintenance in KSTP-II. 4.

Road safety was a major challenge on many of Kerala’s roads, with high rates of motorization3 and a 27 percent increase in the number of traffic fatalities from (3,200 to 4,100) between 2005 and 2011, despite a reduction in road crashes over the same period. In 2012, Kerala had the second highest crash and injury rates in the country 4, and a fatality rate higher than the national average; vulnerable road users – pedestrians, motor cyclists, riders of other two-wheel vehicles – comprised almost three-fourths of the fatalities necessitating a hard look. The Road Safety Authority and the Road Safety Fund that were set up under KSTP needed a mechanism for monitoring, to facilitate evidence-based interventions for improving road safety. While significant efforts at strengthening the institutional structure had been taken under KSTP, further efforts were required to integrate these within a wider institutional 1 48 percent as of 2018-19, as per Economic Review 2021, Government of Kerala, March 2022, Kerala State Planning Board. 2 Road density (528.8 km/100 sq.km) in Kerala is highest in the country, above the national average (387 km/100 sq.km). An operational asset management system was important to get an accurate picture of road conditions and maintenance priorities. Bank engagement in KSTP and other state highway projects had already contributed to successful institutional transformation. 5. At appraisal, the project was deemed highly relevant to the priorities of Government of India (GoI), GOK, and the World Bank. It was closely aligned with the vision for development outlined in the country’s 12th Five-Year Plan (FY2013–17), which called for “faster, sustainable and more inclusive growth”. It supported GOK’s Draft State Road Development Policy 2009-21, that envisaged all state highways to be designed and converted to two lane carriage ways with paved shoulders; 10 percent of state highways to be upgraded to four lanes (based on needs) and all major district roads to be upgraded to single/intermediate lane roads. It was fully aligned with the World Bank Group’s (WBG’s) India Country Partnership Strategy (CPS) for FY13-17 to support poverty reduction and shared prosperity, and supported the CPS pillar “integration”, which focused on connectivity, the strengthening of market mechanisms, and improving the models for private participation in the highway sector. III. KEY FACTORS THAT AFFECTED IMPLEMENTATION AND OUTCOME A. KEY FACTORS DURING PREPARATION 40. Project design built on KSTP.

The project built on KSTP in terms of continuity of reforms in institutions, systems and processes and carried forward reforms initiated on road safety and institutions. The decision to pilot the PPP approach, given the challenges of financing road development in Kerala may, in retrospect, have been too ambitious. 41. Institutional reforms as a derived impact. KSTP II framed an institutional agenda that reflected reality and advanced reforms initiated during KSTP. The 2018 floods and associated crisis created an opportunity for redefining the core road network and streamlining the institutional structure. However, institutional reform was expected to be a derived outcome from the capacity enhancement and road safety activities. As a result, the PDO and the PDO indicators did not specifically include institutional reform directly. 42. Adequacy of risk assessment and mitigation measures. The overall implementation risks were rated as Substantial, and suitable mitigation measures were proposed. At least three of the risks identified (staffing and staff turnover at PWD and RSA, PPP project not being successful, governance challenges including delayed decision making and contract related issues) materialized. One of the mitigation measures to address inadequate market response to PPP was to continue with traditional contract modes. The design of the project was however not flexible enough for such a change without project restructuring. B. KEY FACTORS DURING IMPLEMENTATION 43.

Restructurings and proactivity. As indicated in the Data Sheet and discussed in the section on Significant Changes during Implementation, the project was restructured five times. The Bank team was proactive in responding to the changing circumstances. As discussed in the Efficacy section and under Key Factors during Project Preparation, the PDO was sound but did not reflect the institutions agenda explicitly. The Theory of Change accordingly did not also directly include an indicator on institutional strengthening. PDO indicators on number of beneficiaries and travel time reduction in hindsight, appear less relevant. While the number of beneficiaries including percentage women was considered an appropriate “core” indicator at the time, in hindsight it was difficult to measure the number of beneficiaries from the project unless blanket assumptions were used. A more meaningful indicator on women could have been included, given the high percentage of women engineers in the state (and on the project). On travel time, in retrospect this indicator appears to provide a perverse incentive towards speeding (with implications for road safety). However, at the time the project was designed the general thinking was that this was an appropriate indicator to measure improved traffic flow for a state highway improvement project and thus the team cannot be faulted for including it. The indicators on travel time and reduction in annual fatality counts could also have been worded slightly more clearly to reflect that the variables (and not reductions therein) were being measured.

During the restructuring in June 2019, an outcome indicator to measure the PDO objective relating to enhancing resilience to climate change and disaster risk was appropriately included. The development outcomes achieved under the project are expected to be maintained. The key risks to sustaining these outcomes are with respect to preserving the built infrastructure, sustaining RMMS and institutions like the COE established under the project, and the road safety initiatives undertaken.

The likelihood of these risks materializing is low given GOK’s strong commitment to them, and because some of these (in particular, RMMS) are well aligned with RKI. The COE too is a high priority for GOK, and is considered an important step to ensuring a resilient road infrastructure in Kerala. It is eventually expected to make the transition to a fully autonomous professionally administered body. The setting up of a ‘climate cell’ within the COE also augurs well for its eventual role in helping coordinate and build a comprehensive climate-resilient road infrastructure development strategy for the state. RMMS, if used effectively, is expected to produce data that will enable the state to take informed decisions regarding the maintenance of the corridors constructed under the project. Capacity already built within the KRSA is expected to be maintained, and will institutionalize road safety. The community involvement in road safety initiatives and outcomes bodes well for their sustainability. V. LESSONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS 67. The opportunity to converge with concurrent state level programs is a significant one, and can lend itself to wider impacts.

KSTP-II, working in tandem with the concurrent Resilient Kerala Investment operation amply demonstrated: (a) institutionalizing use of climate data in highway planning and management process; (b) developing a climate smart asset management system; and (c) introducing long term performance contracting with climate/disaster response module. The project contributed significantly, post the 2019 restructuring, to mainstreaming climate resilience in road transport planning and asset management through climate and disaster screening, preparation of DPRs of 500 km of the flood/landslide impacted roads, and development of institutional capabilities in climate mainstreaming in planning, design and asset management, through the COE consultancy. KSTP PMU’s deep involvement in RKI project formulation helped the mainstreaming and integration process, and this Page 24 of 51 The World Bank India Second Kerala State Transport Project (P130339) opportunity to integrate with a concurrent state level program is a significant one that can extend and deepen reforms and desired outcomes. 68. Road safety management improves with result monitoring, community engagement and a bottom-up approach. The project amply demonstrated the value of community engagement derived from extensive involvement of village/neighborhood level/school faculty and students in decision making on interventions and community monitoring at 17 locations on the road safety demonstration corridor.

The decision to involve the local planning agency and think tank National Transportation Planning and Research Center (NATPAC) in developing evidence-based road safety interventions and customizing road safety standards to local requirements paid off well in terms of enhancing road safety outcomes for vulnerable road users. The project also contributed to creation of the TSG in the Road Safety Authority which evidently helped improved monitoring of the road safety activities and also catalyzed coordination among road safety stakeholders. There is scope for replication of the kind of consultation committees constituted under the project, across Kerala and other states, as these would not only help in infrastructure improvements, but also spread road safety awareness to communities, enabling them to have an important say in pertinent road safety issues. 69. KSTP-II offers clues for the future design of future road safety incentive schemes. A further lesson from the Challenge Fund experience is to have more systematic capacity building and training in road safety at the district (and perhaps city) levels so that district/city level officials can identify and prioritize their corridors and formulate solid proposals, as road safety management is still in its infancy at these levels.

Such Challenge Fund sub-components could be perhaps done in two stages: in the first stage, districts be given systematic training and consulting support followed by a competition to submit proposals (similar to the Atal Mission for Rejuvenation and Urban Transformation Scheme or Smart Cities Mission under the national level), and a second stage for actual funding and implementation of proposals from selected districts. 70. Well-designed project components can well support comprehensive institutional development, even if not explicitly included in project design. The project components of road rehabilitation, road safety and subsequently introduced climate and disaster resilience significantly helped improve the planning, asset management and safety capabilities in the sector. The project supported COE also strengthened and influenced inherent institutional capability of better mainstreaming climate and disaster screening, assessment and data in project planning and asset management. In the area of road safety, embedding the TSG in the Road Safety Authority enhanced M&E capability of the sector. These developments clearly indicate how well-designed project components could well influence the institutions, processes and systems if the design of the components have mainstreaming objectives, going beyond the strict boundary of the project. 71. It is important to take early steps to enable a vibrant contracting industry.

The project faced the dual challenges of attracting outside contractors due to artificial entry barriers, and sub-optimal capacity of its local contractors. In addition, about 50 percent of packages were awarded to one contractor (either individually or through JV) which resulted in the contractor’s finances spreading thin thereby causing delays in completion of works. Lowering entry barriers, helping build capacity in the contracting industry, establishing appropriate ceilings on the number of contracts that a contractor can bid for either individually or through joint-venture are all steps that can help build a strong and vibrant contracting industry. . chunks.text: BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS 1. The Project as envisaged during conception was to build roads with improved riding quality and at the same time make it safe for road users. KSTP has no doubt that this was achieved to the satisfaction as anticipated. 2. Component A 1 was delayed mainly on account of Land Acquisition in two packages and Contractors capacity to execute the quantum of work due to cash flow issues. KSTP under the dynamic leadership of Project Director and Chief Engineer never faltered in administration delays hampering the progress of works. 3. The only unanticipated issue would like to highlight is that there was no planning to include “Maintenance” especially for Component A 1 which would have been a boon for the assets created. All these packages were awarded on “Item Rate” basis. 4. Component A 2 was awarded on EPC basis with lot of reluctance from Contractors. The Contractors being mostly from within the State were not very EPC mode friendly. However with insistence from the Government to adopt EPC mode, the Contractors participated and as on date their capacity has been enhanced without any regrets. 5. Creation of JVs as per WB procurement guidelines gave all the smaller Contractors to scale up to higher levels and tremendously increased their morale to rise up to the Quality standards.

chunks.section_path: 5. BORROWER, CO-FINANCIER AND OTHER PARTNER/STAKEHOLDER COMMENTS
chunks.text: The roads executed clearly showed a marked improvement in Quality standards as inferred from road user surveys compared to the roads undertaken by PWD routine works. It also created an awareness and solidarity among Contractors to own the assets with pride as maintenance was a part of these packages for five years. All these were first time experience for the Contractors and also KSTP. This concept has not only given pride to the organization but at the same time enhanced the capacity of KSTP in dealing with large Value contracts in most efficient method. 6. SCDP implementation was a great success in respect to safety. Never before there was any deep insight as to what and how safety can play a vital role in road users. KSTP acknowledges the Banks initiative to implement this work and grateful for the outcome. Implementing other five roads with this concept of safety failed as there are no dedicated Contractors and KSTP had to depend on the Civil Contractors. Participation was very limited and KSTP was forced to retender with time and cost overruns. It is felt that there must be a capacity building to promote dedicated Contractors with safety implementation as prime job. This is still a challenge and hope that it will be accomplished in due course of time. 7. A valuable lesson learnt was how natural disasters can erode the assets created with so much investments in no time.
